# Tools and alternatives

Every tool Slatehire names, scored by the shared method (`COMPARISON-METHOD.md` in the hub): six weighted criteria (fit 35, setup effort 15, reliability and upkeep 15, cost 15, data control 10, integration depth 10), each 0 to 100 with a written evidence line. Closeness is the alternative's fit divided by the reference tool's fit. These are judgements from sources and our own adapter work, not benchmarks. No prices are quoted. Several scores come from general knowledge and say so.

<!-- SCORES:START (generated by tools/score_tools.py, do not edit by hand) -->

Scores dated 2026-11-23. Judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. A tool marked not run was never used against the real vendor.

### Where applicants already live (read only)

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ashby | paid | 80 | 70 | 80 | 55 | 40 | 70 | **69.8** | reference |
| Workable | paid | 75 | 75 | 80 | 55 | 40 | 55 | **67.2** | 94 percent of Ashby |
| Greenhouse | paid | 75 | 60 | 70 | 50 | 40 | 55 | **62.8** | 94 percent of Ashby |
| OpenCATS | open source | 55 | 35 | 45 | 95 | 95 | 0 | **55.0** | 69 percent of Ashby |
| CSV upload and signed webhook | built in | 60 | 95 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **83.8** | 75 percent of Ashby |

What Slatehire has for each: Ashby: Read only candidate.list adapter from the docs, plus a local stand in (not run against Ashby); Workable: Read only candidates adapter from the docs, plus a local stand in (not run against Workable); Greenhouse: Read only Harvest v1 adapter from the docs, plus a local stand in (not run against Greenhouse); OpenCATS: Not supported: no adapter (not run); CSV upload and signed webhook: Built in and tested (run and tested).

**Evidence, Ashby**

- Fit (80): Full applicant records with resume file handles, which is what the first read needs.
- Setup effort (70): An API key from the admin settings. The exact menu path was not on the docs page we read.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Hosted product with a documented, versioned API.
- Cost (55): Paid product for hiring teams. See the vendor price page, no figure is quoted here.
- Data control (40): Candidate data sits with the vendor.
- Integration depth (70): The adapter pages through candidate.list and downloads the resume through a guarded fetch.
- Sources: https://developers.ashbyhq.com/reference/candidatelist (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Workable**

- Fit (75): Candidate list with resume metadata, but the resume link needs a second call that we could not confirm.
- Setup effort (75): Token is made under Integrations in the account menu and is shown once.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): Hosted product with a bearer token API.
- Cost (55): Paid product. See the vendor price page, no figure is quoted here.
- Data control (40): Candidate data sits with the vendor.
- Integration depth (55): The adapter follows paging.next. The resume download step is UNVERIFIED.
- Sources: https://workable.readme.io/reference/generate-an-access-token (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Greenhouse**

- Fit (75): Rich candidate data with attachments, but the v1 and v2 API is announced for removal on 2026-08-31.
- Setup effort (60): Key is made under Configure, Dev Center, API Credential Management and needs a permission few people have.
- Reliability and upkeep (70): Hosted and mature, but an API that is being replaced adds upkeep.
- Cost (50): Paid product aimed at larger teams. See the vendor price page, no figure is quoted here.
- Data control (40): Candidate data sits with the vendor.
- Integration depth (55): The adapter follows the Link header. A v3 adapter is not built.
- Sources: https://docs.greenhouse.io/harvest.html (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, OpenCATS**

- Fit (55): A basic applicant tracker. Written from memory, UNVERIFIED: no API we could rely on was checked.
- Setup effort (35): You host a PHP and MySQL application yourself.
- Reliability and upkeep (45): Updates are slow and security is your job.
- Cost (95): No license cost, you pay for the server.
- Data control (95): Everything stays on your server.
- Integration depth (0): No adapter is built. Use CSV export and upload.
- Sources: https://github.com/opencats/OpenCATS (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, CSV upload and signed webhook**

- Fit (60): Gets applicants in from any system that can export a file or post a signed message.
- Setup effort (95): No account and no keys.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Fewer moving parts than a live connection.
- Cost (100): No licence or usage cost, only the server you already run.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves your server.
- Integration depth (100): Fully built and tested.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/slatehire (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Start with CSV upload or a pasted resume. It needs no account and nothing can change in your ATS.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Pick the ATS your client already uses. All three adapters only read, were written from the vendor docs and ran only against local stand ins.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** CSV and the signed webhook cost nothing. Read each vendor price page yourself, none is quoted here.
- **When open source is the right call:** OpenCATS is the right call for a very small team that wants its own server and accepts an older interface. It is the wrong call when the client wants hosted support and an app they can use on a phone.

### Interview invites

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google Calendar | paid | 80 | 45 | 90 | 80 | 40 | 65 | **70.8** | reference |
| Cal.com | open source | 75 | 60 | 70 | 80 | 85 | 70 | **73.2** | 94 percent of Google Calendar |
| Stay in the app | built in | 40 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **79.0** | 50 percent of Google Calendar |

What Slatehire has for each: Google Calendar: Event insert adapter from the docs, plus a local stand in (not run against Google); Cal.com: Booking adapter from the docs, plus a local stand in (not run against Cal.com); Stay in the app: Built in and tested (the default) (run and tested).

**Evidence, Google Calendar**

- Fit (80): Creates an event with attendees on a calendar people already use.
- Setup effort (45): Needs an OAuth token. Getting one is the hard part and is not automated here.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Mature and widely used.
- Cost (80): Free with an account for personal use. See the vendor page for business plans.
- Data control (40): Data sits with Google.
- Integration depth (65): Creates events only. It does not read availability.
- Sources: https://developers.google.com/calendar (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Cal.com**

- Fit (75): Books a slot for a candidate and interviewers through one call.
- Setup effort (60): API key and an event type id. Where they live in the dashboard was not confirmed.
- Reliability and upkeep (70): Active project. Hosting it yourself adds upkeep.
- Cost (80): Free to self host. A hosted plan has a price page.
- Data control (85): Can run on your own server.
- Integration depth (70): POST /bookings with the version header, tested on a local stand in.
- Sources: https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2 (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Stay in the app**

- Fit (40): Records the plan only. You send the invite yourself.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up: it is the default and works at once.
- Reliability and upkeep (100): Nothing outside the app can fail, because nothing is sent.
- Cost (100): No cost at all, since no outside service is used.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves your server.
- Integration depth (100): Fully built: the plan is saved and the invite is marked as kept in the app.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/slatehire (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Leave invites in the app at first (the default) and send the invite from your own calendar. Nothing is sent by mistake.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Cal.com and Google Calendar adapters send only in live mode with a confirm. Both were written from docs and ran only against local stand ins.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Google Calendar is free with a Google account. Cal.com can be hosted by you. Read the price pages yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Cal.com is the right call when the client wants scheduling on their own server. It is the wrong call when everyone already lives in Google Calendar.

### Where an approved offer goes to be signed

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Breezedoc | paid | 65 | 80 | 75 | 70 | 40 | 10 | **61.5** | reference |
| Documenso | open source | 65 | 45 | 60 | 85 | 95 | 10 | **61.8** | 100 percent of Breezedoc |
| DocuSign | paid | 85 | 50 | 90 | 35 | 35 | 10 | **60.5** | 131 percent of Breezedoc |
| Offer file | built in | 60 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **86.0** | 92 percent of Breezedoc |

What Slatehire has for each: Breezedoc: Not built: the API could not be confirmed. The file hand off is the path (not run); Documenso: Not built: file hand off only (not run); DocuSign: Not built: file hand off only (not run); Offer file: Built in and tested (the default) (run and tested).

**Evidence, Breezedoc**

- Fit (65): Simple document signing for small teams. We could not confirm what its API offers.
- Setup effort (80): Sign in and upload a file.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): A hosted product, but we could not check its uptime or API history.
- Cost (70): Paid with a free tier reported. See the vendor page, no figure is quoted here.
- Data control (40): Documents sit with the vendor.
- Integration depth (10): No live call is built. The page we fetched was a login page.
- Sources: https://breezedoc.com/integrations/api (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Documenso**

- Fit (65): Open source signing with an API, not checked by us for this use.
- Setup effort (45): Self hosting needs Docker and a database.
- Reliability and upkeep (60): Young project. Upkeep is yours when self hosted.
- Cost (85): Free to self host, you pay for the server it runs on.
- Data control (95): Documents stay on your server.
- Integration depth (10): No adapter is built.
- Sources: https://documenso.com (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, DocuSign**

- Fit (85): The best known signing tool, accepted almost everywhere.
- Setup effort (50): Needs an account and templates.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Mature and widely relied on, judged from general knowledge only.
- Cost (35): Priced per seat and per envelope on its price page. No figure is quoted here.
- Data control (35): Documents sit with the vendor.
- Integration depth (10): No adapter is built. Written from general knowledge, UNVERIFIED.
- Sources: https://www.docusign.com (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Offer file**

- Fit (60): A plain text file of the approved offer for any signing tool.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up: the file is written to the export folder.
- Reliability and upkeep (100): A file cannot fail to send.
- Cost (100): No cost, it is a text file on your own disk.
- Data control (100): Stays on your server.
- Integration depth (100): Fully built and tested, and the file name carries the candidate code.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/slatehire (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the offer file: open it in your signing tool and send it from there. Slatehire never sends an offer.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** No live signing call is built for any of these. The offer text is a file you paste in. Check each tool for what it can import.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** The file hand off costs nothing. Documenso is open source. Read the other price pages yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Documenso is the right call when signed contracts must stay on your own server. It is the wrong call when the client already has DocuSign and wants nothing new.

### Where application emails arrive

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IMAP mailbox | open standard | 70 | 70 | 75 | 100 | 70 | 80 | **76.2** | reference |
| Gmail (through IMAP) | paid | 70 | 60 | 85 | 80 | 40 | 60 | **68.2** | 100 percent of IMAP mailbox |
| Signed webhook | built in | 60 | 70 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **80.0** | 86 percent of IMAP mailbox |

What Slatehire has for each: IMAP mailbox: Built and tested against a local fake mail server (run against a local stand in only); Gmail (through IMAP): Works through the IMAP adapter, not run live (not run against Gmail); Signed webhook: Built and tested (run and tested).

**Evidence, IMAP mailbox**

- Fit (70): Reads application emails and attachments from a shared inbox.
- Setup effort (70): Needs host, user and an app password. Two step verification must be on for Gmail.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Standard protocol. Providers change sign in rules now and then.
- Cost (100): No extra cost beyond the mailbox you already have.
- Data control (70): Mail stays with the provider, Slatehire keeps only what it reads.
- Integration depth (80): Reads only mail whose subject has the word Application, and marks a message read only after it was dealt with.
- Sources: https://support.google.com/mail (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Gmail (through IMAP)**

- Fit (70): Common for small companies.
- Setup effort (60): App password at myaccount.google.com/apppasswords.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Mature and stable, though sign in rules for apps change from time to time.
- Cost (80): Free for personal accounts. See the vendor page for business plans.
- Data control (40): Data sits with Google.
- Integration depth (60): Used through IMAP only. No Gmail API.
- Sources: https://support.google.com/mail (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Signed webhook**

- Fit (60): One applicant per message from any form or ATS that can post JSON.
- Setup effort (70): Needs a shared secret on both sides.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): A signature check and size limit on every message.
- Cost (100): No cost, it is one route of the app itself.
- Data control (100): Nothing extra leaves your server.
- Integration depth (100): Fully built and tested.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/slatehire (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Start with the demo inbox, then CSV. Connect a mailbox only when you are ready.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Plain IMAP works with Gmail (app password), Outlook and most hosts, and was tested against a local fake server. It only reads.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** IMAP is free with the mailbox you already have.
- **When open source is the right call:** Not a paid versus open source choice: IMAP is an open standard. A mailbox shared by many people may fit a form tool and the signed webhook better.

### What reads the redacted resume

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A language model (Anthropic API) | paid | 80 | 60 | 70 | 55 | 40 | 60 | **65.8** | reference |
| Offline rules scorer | built in | 60 | 100 | 90 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **84.5** | 75 percent of A language model (Anthropic API) |

What Slatehire has for each: A language model (Anthropic API): Built behind the shared wrapper (SCORER=model), UNVERIFIED live (run against a local stand in only); Offline rules scorer: Built and tested on a held out set (run and tested).

**Evidence, A language model (Anthropic API)**

- Fit (80): Reads messy text better than rules. Its answers must still pass the quote check.
- Setup effort (60): Needs an API key and a prompt that treats resumes as untrusted text.
- Reliability and upkeep (70): Answers can differ run to run, so consistency is a test, not a given.
- Cost (55): Billed per use. See the vendor price page.
- Data control (40): Resume text would be sent to the vendor, which needs a privacy decision.
- Integration depth (60): Built behind the shared model wrapper, one criterion per call, every quote and the total checked by code. Run only against a local fake server.
- Sources: https://docs.anthropic.com (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Offline rules scorer**

- Fit (60): Finds the criteria words and the sentences around them. It misses what it has no words for.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up: it ships with the app and needs no key.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Same text, same score, every time.
- Cost (100): No cost, it runs on your own server with no outside call.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves your server.
- Integration depth (100): Fully built, with verbatim quote checks.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/slatehire (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the offline rules scorer. It is plain, repeatable and every quote is checked by code.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** A language model can replace the proposal step and the quote check still applies. That path is built behind the shared model wrapper and tested against a local fake server and recorded fixtures; it was never run with a real key (UNVERIFIED live).
- **Cost sensitive owner:** The offline scorer costs nothing. A model is billed per use on the vendor price page.
- **When open source is the right call:** The rules scorer is the right call when a hiring decision must be explainable word for word. It is the wrong call when resumes are long, messy or in many languages.

### Where the data is stored

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | open source | 90 | 60 | 90 | 80 | 90 | 90 | **84.0** | reference |
| SQLite | open source | 70 | 100 | 85 | 100 | 100 | 90 | **86.2** | 78 percent of PostgreSQL |

What Slatehire has for each: PostgreSQL: Built, migration cycle run on a throwaway server (run (migrations)); SQLite: Built (the demo default) (run and tested).

**Evidence, PostgreSQL**

- Fit (90): Handles many users and the job queue.
- Setup effort (60): Needs a server, or your host adds one.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Mature and well understood, with a long record in production.
- Cost (80): Free software. Hosting is billed by your host.
- Data control (90): You hold the data, wherever you choose to host the server.
- Integration depth (90): The default for deploys.
- Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, SQLite**

- Fit (70): Enough for one user.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to set up: it is a single file next to the app.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Very stable, one writer at a time.
- Cost (100): No cost, and no server to pay for.
- Data control (100): One file on your disk.
- Integration depth (90): Same models as Postgres.
- Sources: https://www.sqlite.org/docs.html (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** SQLite for the demo and a single machine. Nothing to install.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Postgres for any real deployment. The migrations were run up, down and up on both.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** SQLite is free and a file. Postgres is free software and your host charges for it.
- **When open source is the right call:** Both are open source. SQLite is the right call for one user on one machine. It is the wrong call when several services write at once.

### Where the app runs

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Railway | paid | 80 | 80 | 75 | 60 | 40 | 70 | **71.2** | reference |
| Vercel | paid | 80 | 85 | 85 | 60 | 40 | 70 | **73.5** | 100 percent of Railway |
| Hetzner | paid | 80 | 40 | 60 | 90 | 90 | 70 | **72.5** | 100 percent of Railway |

What Slatehire has for each: Railway: Dockerfiles and a config file, never deployed (not run on Railway); Vercel: Next.js web app settings, never deployed (not run on Vercel); Hetzner: Docker Compose, Caddy and a cloud init file, never deployed (not run on Hetzner).

**Evidence, Railway**

- Fit (80): Runs the API, the worker and Postgres from one repo.
- Setup effort (80): Connect the repo and set variables.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Hosted. Config as code is deprecated, so settings live in the dashboard.
- Cost (60): Billed by use. See the vendor price page.
- Data control (40): Data sits on their servers.
- Integration depth (70): Dockerfile paths and a health check are set.
- Sources: https://docs.railway.com (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Vercel**

- Fit (80): Best fit for the Next.js web app only.
- Setup effort (85): Import the repo, set the root to apps/web.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Hosted, previews and rollback.
- Cost (60): A free tier exists. See the vendor price page.
- Data control (40): Pages and logs sit with the vendor.
- Integration depth (70): Set API_BASE_URL and SESSION_SECRET.
- Sources: https://vercel.com/docs (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Hetzner**

- Fit (80): One server runs the whole system.
- Setup effort (40): You manage the server, the firewall and updates.
- Reliability and upkeep (60): Reliability is your job.
- Cost (90): Usually the cheapest. See the vendor price page.
- Data control (90): You hold the server.
- Integration depth (70): Compose, Caddy and a backup script are written.
- Sources: https://docs.hetzner.com (checked 2026-11-23)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Run it on your own computer with the demo first. When ready, Vercel for the web app and Railway for the API is the easiest pair.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Vercel and Railway are the easiest. Hetzner with Docker Compose is the cheapest and most controlled. Nothing here was deployed to a real account.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A small Hetzner server runs everything. Read the vendor price pages yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** A Hetzner server is the right call when you want one bill and full control and can manage updates. It is the wrong call when nobody will watch the server.

### Named but not scored

- Cloudflare Tunnel and Cloudflare DNS: Named in the deploy guides for webhook testing and a custom domain. Infrastructure, not a choice Slatehire depends on.
- Anthropic API as a live scorer: Scored above as a language model option. The live path is built and only run against a local fake server (UNVERIFIED live).
